https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9p8.text: Image source, Reuters By Jack Burgess Â and Â Toby Mann Published 18 October 2026 Updated 3 hours ago US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table. "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table". Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened. Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake". Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed. In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now". Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%. In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders". Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ukraine's President Zelensky attended an EU leaders' summit in Brussels on Friday Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia. Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war. The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks. Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues. However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds. Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence. Mark Hallam Lyon's tourism office on the Place Bellecour was set ablaze over the weekend [FILE: October 17, 2026] Image: Jeff Pachoud/AFP At least four other cities — Lyon, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille — have announced continued localized restrictions that will take effect on Tuesday night. In Lyon, the prefect of the Rhone region, ordered another curfew from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. in what's known colloquially as the hypercentre of the old city — an area spanning the first and second Arondissements and other key historic zones like the city hall, the Place Bellecour pedestrian square and the commercial and historic neighborhood Les Cordeliers. Prefect Etienne Guyot also said a ban on what French authorities term attroupements — gatherings of people deemed to have the potential to threaten public order — from 4 p.m. until 9 p.m. would also apply. In Bordeaux, unaccompanied minors will not be allowed on the streets from 10 p.m. until 7 a.m. "in the sectors particularly affected by the pillages of October 17," Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas said. She said this was aimed to "prevent all new attacks on businesses" in a series of key central streets and squares. The restrictions were set to apply until next Monday, October 26. And to the south in Nice, the city center sector, the old city and the Trachel-Gare du Sud sectors will be restricted from 9 p.m. until 6 a.m. until Sunday, October 25. "The deployment for next Saturday will be massive," Lecornu said in the National Assembly. He said the security operation last weekend had been "too static and not mobile enough." Lecornu said adequate support for security forces was "the precondition for everything" when trying to both allow peaceful protests but also keep order, saying that "1,000 injured police and gendarmes over the weekend" nationwide was unacceptable. Lecornu said the national public message in response should convey to them "clear, frank and massive support." The prime minister also accused what he referred to as small ultra-left and extreme-left groups in certain locations of forging an "insurrectionary plan" that fueled the violent rioting over the weekend for which the government could provide evidence. "What happened at the mayoral office of Limoges was an example. You have a first arrest that was carried out this morning," Lecornu said. Shared mobility operator Dott, in a statement to Reuters on Monday, said that about 300 of its electric bikes were destroyed and 120 severely damaged in Paris, during the nationwide anti-government protests on Saturday. It estimates the damage at about €400,000 ($450,000). Lime, another entity for shared electric bikes, said 6% of its Paris fleet was destroyed or damaged. Ahead of demonstrations, Lime said it worked with the police to remove vehicles from designated protest routes and restricted parking or riding in high-risk areas. Smovengo, operator ​of the Vélib' Métropole bike-sharing service in Paris, told Reuters that some 300 of its 20,000 bike fleet were damaged or stolen over the weekend.
